tldr: This paper shows how to distill the latent behavior space of a Behavior Foundation Model trained on a single robot into other humanoids in under 1 GPU-hour using motion retargeting correspondences, achieving whole-body control via a shared latent vector.
hero_caption: An overview of the CrossBFM concept. By sharing a single pretrained latent behavior space across multiple robots, the same latent vector can control different robot embodiments as intended—spanning motion tracking, goal reaching, reward optimization, and generative motion prompting.
overview:
Introducing Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) to humanoid robots allows diverse instructions—such as motion tracking, reaching target poses, and maximizing specified rewards—using just a single latent vector. However, conventional training based on Forward-Backward (FB) representations consumes hundreds of GPU-hours per robot. Repeating this training from scratch for another robot produces a geometrically unrelated latent space, making knowledge sharing and transfer across embodiments difficult.

To address this, the authors realized that instead of running heavy reinforcement learning from scratch for every robot, they could simply treat the existing robot's latent space as a coordinate system and distill it into other robots. Motion retargeting from human motion capture data to various robots provides frame-level correspondences across embodiments. Using these correspondences as ground truth labels, a unified encoder with no robot-specific parameters maps observations into the latent space via supervised regression.

In experiments, the authors distilled a space pretrained on the Unitree G1 into three different humanoids and evaluated it under diverse conditions, including real-world hardware. The unified encoder trained in less than 1 GPU-hour, and control policies for each embodiment finished training in about 10 GPU-hours. The resulting policy achieved high-precision motion tracking, smooth pose transitions, and reward optimization on par with conventional direct joint-command baselines.
contributions: Proposed a robot-agnostic unified encoder architecture that distills multiple humanoids with different embodiments into a single shared latent space in less than an hour.
Formulated cross-embodiment latent space transfer as a supervised regression task by leveraging frame-level correspondences provided by motion retargeting.

Built whole-body trackers conditioned on the distilled shared latent space and demonstrated that all three prompting modes—motion tracking, goal reaching, and reward optimization—transfer to other robots, validated on real hardware.
Demonstrated data scaling properties showing robust performance with only 25% of motion data, as well as zero-shot generalization capabilities to morphologically similar unseen robots.

sections.heading: Ending the Era of Retraining Humanoids From Scratch
sections.summary: Conventional Behavior Foundation Models train latent spaces independently for each robot at immense computational cost, preventing space sharing and transfer. This paper proposes CrossBFM, using retargeted data to ultra-fast distill an existing latent space to other robots.
sections.details:
Reinforcement learning has driven remarkable progress in humanoid whole-body control. However, many policies require dense joint-space trajectory references, making goal specification cumbersome for complex tasks. Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) using Forward-Backward (FB) representations emerged as an appealing solution. With them, passing a single vector $z$ sampled from a latent space executes motion tracking, goal pose reaching, and reward maximization without any retraining.

Yet, major challenges remain: massive compute is needed for each robot, and the resulting latent spaces remain disjoint across embodiments. Prior work such as BFM-Zero requires over 100 GPU-hours per training run. Moreover, training from scratch for each new robot yields latent spaces that do not align in coordinate meaning, even if their geometric topologies appear similar.

CrossBFM treats the BFM latent space pretrained on the Unitree G1 as a fixed behavior coordinate system and distills it into other robots. Because retargeted motions derived from the same mocap corpus provide frame-to-frame correspondences across robots at identical timestamps, the network can project a new robot's proprioception into the shared latent space through simple supervised regression, bypassing simulator trial-and-error and adversarial training entirely.

sections.heading: Merging Behavior Foundation Models With Cross-Embodiment Learning
sections.summary: The paper contextualizes three research lines: RL-based whole-body control, cross-embodiment learning across morphological gaps, and motion retargeting with knowledge distillation. CrossBFM stands out by directly inheriting a value-function-grounded latent space.
sections.details:
### Humanoid Control and Unsupervised RL
Traditional whole-body control predominantly uses PPO to track joint-space trajectories. However, this demands fine-grained joint targets at every frame. In contrast, unsupervised RL based on FB representations treats latent vectors as behavior descriptors, analytically mapping reward functions or goal poses into latent vectors. While BFM-Zero and UFO advanced this direction, both construct separate latent spaces per embodiment without considering cross-robot transfer.

### Cross-Embodiment Learning
To learn a single policy across different robots, prior approaches tokenize morphologies using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) or Transformers. However, these methods are often restricted to single tasks like locomotion and cannot embed general-purpose behaviors into a latent space—such as maximizing an arbitrary reward or reaching specified poses—as BFMs do. Recent efforts exploring shared latent spaces also treat latents merely as descriptive representations, lacking the analytical formulation needed to derive latents directly from rewards.

### Retargeting and Knowledge Distillation
This work recognizes that high-quality motion retargeting already provides frame-level cross-embodiment correspondence. Treating this correspondence as an oracle, the framework efficiently distills latent variables from a source teacher model into target student robots.

sections.heading: How Latent Vectors Become Universal Prompts: FB Representations
sections.summary: This section introduces successor measures and their low-rank FB representations, explaining mathematically why a learned backward map can instantaneously convert arbitrary reward functions and goal poses into latent vectors.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Unsupervised RL and Successor Measures
In a reward-free Markov Decision Process, an agent learns the dynamics governing long-term state transitions under its policy. With successor measures, the value function for any reward function $r$ decomposes into the product of the measure over future visited states and the reward at those states.

### 3.2 Forward-Backward Representations
The FB representation approximates this successor measure with a low-rank factorization of dimension $d$. It learns a forward map $F$ depending on state, action, and latent vector, alongside a backward map $B$ depending only on state, representing the value function via their inner product. The key advantage is that the optimal latent vector $z$ for any reward function $r$ can be computed analytically in closed form as an expectation under the backward map $B$.

### 3.3 Three Prompting Modes
With a trained backward map $B$, three modes of control can be executed without retraining:
- **Motion tracking**: Latent vectors are computed as lookahead embeddings of a reference motion sequence and passed to the policy.
- **Goal reaching**: For a desired goal state $s_g$, setting $z_g = \mathrm{proj}(B(s_g))$ drives smooth pose transitions.
- **Reward optimization**: Computing $z_{\mathrm{rew}}$ as a reward-weighted average over sampled states guides the policy to maximize that reward.
Thus, once a mapping corresponding to the backward map $B$ is acquired for a new robot, all three prompting capabilities become immediately accessible.

sections.heading: Unified Encoder and Controller Bridged by Retargeting
sections.summary: Freezing the Unitree G1 latent space, the authors propose a unified encoder that projects each robot's proprioception into the shared space. A 163-dimensional fixed slot design with masks absorbs morphology gaps, after which per-robot PPO trackers are trained.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Overall Setup and Notation
The backward map $B_S$ of the BFM trained on the Unitree G1 is frozen, using its latent space (dimension $d=256$, hypersphere $\mathcal{Z}$ with radius $\sqrt{d}$) as the shared coordinate system. For each robot $X$, retargeted motion frames $o_t^X$ are paired with ground-truth latent vectors $z_t^\star$ obtained from corresponding G1 frames to form training pairs for the encoder.

### 4.2 Unified Encoder Architecture
If input dimensions varied across robots, distinct models would be required, preventing shared representations from forming and hindering generalization to unseen robots. To solve this, the authors designed a uniform 163-dimensional input shared by all robots. It includes 8 key-body parts (knees, ankles, elbows, etc.), 33 standardized joint slots, and pelvic pose and velocity information. For joints or bodies absent in a given robot, a binary mask accompanies zero-padding, enabling the network to clearly distinguish between a zero angle and an absent joint.

### 4.3 Phase 1: Regressing the Backward Map
The encoder uses a Transformer with causal attention. It references only past frames within a temporal window to predict each frame's latent vector, projecting it onto the hypersphere. The training objective is simple cosine distance against the ground-truth latent vector $z_t^\star$. This supervised regression finishes in under 1 GPU-hour on an RTX 4090.

### 4.4 Phase 2: Latent-Conditioned Control Policies
Conditioned on the distilled latent space, control policies are trained for each embodiment using PPO. The actor receives only the latent vector $z$ and the robot's proprioceptive observations without direct joint references. Privileged reference information in simulation is provided solely to the critic in an asymmetric design. Additionally, a flow-based generative model is introduced to sample motion chunks directly within this shared latent space.

### 4.5 Deployment: Prompt Execution on Target Robots
Motion tracking and goal reaching work directly with latents $z$ produced by the trained encoder. Reward optimization, however, faces embodiment-dependent physical limits (e.g., a compact humanoid cannot reach an arm height of 1.0 m). To handle this, the authors propose marginal transport by matching quantiles of the cumulative distribution function (CDF) for key-body features in each robot's retargeting data. This automatically scales reward prompts to each robot's physique.

sections.heading: Succeeding With Only 25% Data and Transferring to Unseen Robots
sections.summary: Using three humanoid models (M3, T1, N1), the authors thoroughly evaluate the three prompting modes, generalization to unseen motions, data scaling limits, zero-shot transfer to unseen embodiments, and real-world hardware deployment.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Transfer of Three Prompting Modes
Compared to a joint-space tracking baseline (TWIST2), the latent-conditioned policy tracking error fell behind by only $0.025$ rad. While the joint-tracking baseline suffered from torque spikes and falls when target poses changed abruptly, CrossBFM performed smooth goal reaching without falling by interpolating within the latent space. Across 41 reward prompts, CrossBFM with quantile mapping achieved more than 3x higher returns than directly reusing the source robot's latent vectors.

### 5.2 Latent Inference on Unseen Motions
When evaluated on an unseen validation motion dataset, key-body tracking error increased by only 1.4 to 6.7 mm. t-SNE visualizations of the latent space confirmed that unseen clips cleanly clustered into their respective behavior categories.

### 5.3 Data Scaling Properties: A Quarter of Data Suffices
Reducing the training motion corpus to 25% (one quarter) led to only a 5% degradation in joint tracking error (0.2132 rad to 0.2241 rad). Performance dropped sharply only when the dataset was reduced to 10%, proving that the robust geometric structure can be recovered from minimal data.

### 5.4 Generalization to Unseen Embodiments
In a leave-one-out setup where the encoder was trained on two robots and evaluated on a third, including N1 (morphologically close to M3) allowed the encoder to recover 89.3% of seen tracking performance on the unseen M3. Conversely, recovery dropped to 12.8% on T1 due to substantial size disparities, highlighting that morphological proximity is vital for zero-shot generalization.

### 5.5 Real-Robot Verification
All prompting modes were verified on physical M3 and T1 humanoids. The real robots matched simulation results with smooth tracking, pose transitions, reward optimization, and autonomous locomotion and dancing driven by the flow generative model.

sections.heading: Summary and What Lies Ahead
sections.summary: CrossBFM demonstrates that BFM latent spaces can be distilled into other robots quickly and accurately using retargeted data. Future directions include scaling data diversity and exploring text-prompted long-horizon planning.
sections.details:
This work introduced CrossBFM, treating a pretrained Behavior Foundation Model's latent space as a shared behavioral coordinate frame and distilling it into other humanoids through supervised learning over motion retargeting correspondences.

With a unified encoder free of robot-specific weights, high-fidelity latent sharing is achieved in less than an hour of training, enabling motion tracking, goal reaching, and reward optimization on new robots. Furthermore, the geometric integrity is retained with just 25% of motion data, and zero-shot transfer extends to morphologically similar unseen platforms.

For future work, the authors plan to expand training data diversity for higher-resolution latent spaces, investigate scaling laws across broader robot morphologies, and integrate language prompting for long-horizon mobile manipulation tasks.

sections.heading: Appendix: Unified Encoder Architecture and Generative Model Details
sections.summary: Details on the 163-dimensional input specification, architectural decisions like Pre-LayerNorm to avert mode collapse, causal attention benefits, embodiment size normalization, and Rectified Flow motion generation.
sections.details:
### Unified Encoder Architecture
The encoder consists of 4 Transformer blocks with a hidden dimension of 256. Using Pre-LayerNorm was essential; Post-LayerNorm led to severe mode collapse where outputs collapsed to a constant value that cosine loss could not recover from. A hypersphere projection layer is placed at the end so gradients backpropagate smoothly.

### Input Specification and Normalization
Input dimensions are fixed at 163 across all robots. Standardized joint ordering, pelvis yaw direction alignment, and scale normalization—dividing coordinates by the nominal pelvis height—allow the encoder to process kinematically diverse robots with geometrically consistent representations.

### Causal Attention for Real-Time Execution
Bidirectional attention looks ahead roughly one second into future frames, restricting it to offline use. Adopting causal attention achieved real-time execution suitable for real-robot teleoperation without degrading tracking accuracy.

### Motion Generation via Rectified Flow
A flow-based model was trained to generate 64-frame latent trajectory chunks on the shared latent space. Conditioned on behavior categories and past latent history, it directly drives whole-body motions on the robot without requiring any explicit joint-space reference trajectories.

takeaways: Retargeted motion datasets act as an effective oracle providing cross-embodiment geometric correspondences for knowledge distillation.
Using a shared latent space as an intermediary avoids abrupt joint torque spikes seen with discontinuous commands, enabling smooth pose transitions.
Transferring Behavior Foundation Models does not require heavy reinforcement learning per embodiment; formulating transfer as regression to a fixed latent space cuts compute time dramatically.
When sharing reward functions across robots with different physical proportions, marginal transport matching CDF percentiles is much more effective than using absolute values.
limitations: Zero-shot transfer remains difficult for humanoids with drastically divergent morphologies (e.g., extreme scale differences or fundamentally different joint configurations).
The approach depends on the quality of retargeting data; extreme kinematic biases or temporal alignment errors degrade encoder inference.
Training the latent-conditioned policy itself still requires about 10 hours of reinforcement learning within a simulator environment (such as MuJoCo) for each robot embodiment.
